title: Deriving and using the wave equation

learning_outcomes.text: derive, using the definitions of speed, frequency and wavelength, the wave equation v = fλ

prior_knowledge_summary: A progressive wave transfers energy while points in the medium oscillate locally.
Frequency is cycles per unit time, wavelength is the shortest distance between adjacent in-phase points, and T = 1/f.
A CRO time-base and cycle count can be used to determine period and frequency.
Distances and times must use compatible units before physical quantities are combined.
new_learning: Derive v = fλ from one wavelength travelled in one period.
Select and rearrange v = fλ consistently with units.
not_yet_taught: comparison of transverse and longitudinal waves
wave intensity and its relationships with power, area or amplitude

blocks.heading: How fast is a pattern we cannot chase?
content: A wave machine produces 6.0 complete cycles each second. Neighbouring crests are 0.40 m apart. Without following one crest with a stopwatch, can we predict how far the pattern moves each second?
Each new cycle sends the pattern forward by one wavelength. Counting cycles and knowing the distance per cycle should therefore reveal the wave speed.

figure.purpose: Create the need to combine cycles per second with distance per cycle.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper teacher sketch of a wave train advancing past a fixed marker. Mark one wavelength and show six small cycle tally marks beside a one-second clock, but do not display the final speed or equation.
figure.alt_text: A wave train advances one wavelength for each cycle counted during one second.

blocks.heading: One cycle carries the pattern one wavelength
content: Definition to learn: wavelength is the minimum distance between two adjacent points on a wave that are in phase. Two neighbouring crests are in phase, so their separation is one wavelength.

Watch one crest for one complete period T. After that time, the wave pattern has advanced to the position previously occupied by the next crest. The distance travelled is λ, so speed = distance/time gives v = λ/T.
This argument follows the moving pattern or wavefront. It does not claim that a particle of the medium travels one wavelength.

controlled_definition.accepted_definition: the minimum distance between two adjacent points on a wave that are in phase

figure.purpose: Show why one period corresponds to one wavelength of pattern travel.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper two-frame sequence of the same progressive wave at time zero and time T. Use a coloured crest marker and a horizontal λ bracket to show the pattern moving one wavelength, while a medium particle remains near its local equilibrium position.
figure.alt_text: Two time frames show a wave crest moving one wavelength during one period while a medium point oscillates locally.

blocks.heading: From period to frequency
content: Definition to learn: frequency is the number of complete oscillations or wave cycles per unit time. Since T = 1/f, substitute 1/f for T in v = λ/T.
Then v = λ/(1/f) = fλ. Formula to remember: v = fλ. Here v is wave speed in m s⁻¹, f is frequency in Hz, and λ is wavelength in m.
The units explain the physics: Hz means s⁻¹, so fλ has unit s⁻¹ × m = m s⁻¹. It is cycles per second multiplied by metres per cycle.

controlled_definition.accepted_definition: the number of complete oscillations or wave cycles per unit time

symbols.v: wave speed in metres per second (m s⁻¹)

figure.purpose: Make the derivation and its unit meaning visible as one causal chain.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper derivation flow: v equals λ divided by T, T equals 1/f, substitution, then v equals fλ. Add a small unit strip showing per second times metres equals metres per second.
figure.alt_text: A derivation flow substitutes T equals one over f into speed equals wavelength over period.

blocks.heading: Use the equation, then check the meaning
content: Return to the wave machine: f = 6.0 Hz and λ = 0.40 m. Choose v = fλ because speed is unknown and frequency and wavelength are known.
Substitute with units: v = 6.0 s⁻¹ × 0.40 m = 2.4 m s⁻¹. The pattern advances 0.40 m six times each second, which is 2.4 m in one second.
An independent check uses one period. T = 1/6.0 s, so λ/T = 0.40/(1/6.0) = 2.4 m s⁻¹. Both routes agree.

figure.purpose: Model equation selection, substitution with units and an independent period check.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper annotated worked layout with knowns f = 6.0 Hz and λ = 0.40 m, the v = fλ route, units carried through, and a separate λ/T check in a different colour.
figure.alt_text: A worked layout obtains 2.4 metres per second and checks it using the period route.

blocks.heading: Rearrange before inserting numbers
content: A ripple travels at 0.72 m s⁻¹ and has frequency 3.0 Hz. Wavelength is unknown. Start from v = fλ and divide both sides by f: λ = v/f.
Now substitute: λ = 0.72 m s⁻¹ / 3.0 s⁻¹ = 0.24 m. The s⁻¹ units cancel, leaving metres, as a wavelength must.
Reverse solving works the same way for frequency: f = v/λ. Write the symbolic rearrangement first, then convert units, substitute and inspect the final unit.

figure.purpose: Teach safe symbolic rearrangement and unit cancellation.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper balance-style equation sketch showing v = fλ becoming λ = v/f, followed by 0.72 m s^-1 divided by 3.0 s^-1 and cancellation to 0.24 m. Include a smaller branch to f = v/λ without numbers.
figure.alt_text: A balance-style rearrangement finds wavelength and shows inverse-second units cancelling.

blocks.heading: The equation cannot repair mixed units
content: It feels safe to insert every displayed number into v = fλ because the formula is correct. The formula is only numerically safe when the units are compatible.
For a wave with f = 2.5 kHz and λ = 12 cm, convert first: 2.5 kHz = 2.5 × 10³ Hz and 12 cm = 0.12 m. Then v = 2.5 × 10³ × 0.12 = 3.0 × 10² m s⁻¹.
Multiplying 2.5 by 12 gives 30, but that number carries kHz cm, not m s⁻¹. A dimensional check exposes the mistake before it becomes an answer.

figure.purpose: Contrast a tempting mixed-unit substitution with the correct SI conversion route.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper comparison table. Left column shows 2.5 times 12 with kHz cm and a warning symbol. Right column converts to 2.5 times ten cubed Hz and 0.12 m before obtaining 3.0 times ten squared m s^-1.
figure.alt_text: A comparison table shows why kilohertz and centimetres must be converted before calculating wave speed.

blocks.heading: A dependable wave-equation route
content: Derivation: in one period the wave pattern travels one wavelength, so v = λ/T. Since T = 1/f, v = fλ.
Calculation: identify the unknown, rearrange symbolically, convert frequency and wavelength to compatible units, substitute with units, then check the result by dimensions or physical meaning.
A CRO may supply the frequency from its time-base. Combining that measured frequency with a known wavelength gives speed. We still do not need to classify the wave or calculate intensity.

figure.purpose: Summarise derivation, rearrangement, unit conversion and the CRO link while locking the boundary.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper decision map: measured period to frequency, wavelength plus frequency to speed, and rearrangement branches for f and λ. End with unit checks and a boundary box that defers wave type and intensity.
figure.alt_text: A decision map links CRO frequency measurement to the wave equation and its three rearrangements.

visual_planning.style: rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch

concepts_taught: one wavelength of pattern travel in one period
selection and rearrangement of the wave equation
misconceptions_addressed: A medium particle travels one wavelength in each period.
Numbers may be substituted before making units compatible.
A rearranged equation is a different physical law.
next_lesson_can_assume: Derive v = fλ from one wavelength travelled in one period.
Convert frequency and wavelength to compatible units before substitution.
Combine a CRO-derived frequency with wavelength to determine wave speed.
next_lesson_must_not_assume: Compare oscillation direction with wave travel direction.
Calculate wave intensity or use intensity-amplitude relationships.
